header:
How to read your
pay stub and W-2

lines.text: Your W-2 can show three different wages. All are right.
lines.say: Your W-2 can show three different wages. All are right.

lines.text: On a $60,000 salary, one box can say $54,400 and two others $57,400.
lines.say: On a sixty thousand dollar salary, one box can say fifty-four thousand four hundred, and two others fifty-seven thousand four hundred.

lines.text: None of them is a typo. Each box answers a different question about the same pay.
lines.say: None of them is a typo. Each box answers a different question about the same pay.

lines.text: In February 2023, 43% of private businesses paid every two weeks. That's 26 pay stubs a year.
lines.say: In February twenty twenty-three, forty-three percent of private businesses paid every two weeks. That's twenty-six pay stubs a year.

lines.text: Most people check the bottom number and move on. The lines above it show where every dollar went.
lines.say: Most people check the bottom number and move on. The lines above it show where every dollar went.

lines.text: The plan: gross to net, the tax lines, one paycheck with exact math, the W-2 box by box, and the common mistakes.
lines.say: Here's the plan: gross to net, the tax lines, one paycheck with exact math, the W-2 box by box, and the common mistakes.

lines.text: Education, not advice. All numbers use 2026 rules.
lines.say: This is education, not advice, and every number uses the twenty twenty-six rules.

lines.text: Chapter 1: Gross to net.
lines.say: Chapter one: gross to net.

lines.text: A pay stub reads top to bottom, and it starts with gross pay.
lines.say: A pay stub reads top to bottom, and it starts with gross pay.

lines.text: Gross pay is everything you earned before anything comes out: salary or hourly pay, plus overtime, bonuses or tips.
lines.say: Gross pay is everything you earned before anything comes out: salary or hourly pay, plus overtime, bonuses or tips.

lines.text: Next come pre-tax deductions. They come out before income tax is figured, so they shrink your taxable pay.
lines.say: Next come the pre-tax deductions. They come out before income tax is figured, so they shrink your taxable pay.

lines.text: Typical pre-tax items: a traditional 401(k), health premiums, HSA or FSA money. Roth 401(k), union dues and garnishments usually come after tax.
lines.say: Typical pre-tax items: a traditional four oh one k, health premiums, and H S A or F S A money. Roth four oh one k, union dues and garnishments usually come after tax.

lines.text: Then the taxes: federal withholding, Social Security, Medicare, and maybe state and local tax.
lines.say: Then the taxes: federal withholding, Social Security, Medicare, and maybe state and local tax.

lines.text: Last come after-tax deductions. What's left is net pay, the money that lands in your account.
lines.say: Last come after-tax deductions. What's left is net pay, the money that lands in your account.

lines.text: In our example later, a $2,307.69 paycheck becomes $1,756.19 of take-home pay.
lines.say: In our example later, a paycheck of about two thousand three hundred eight dollars becomes about one thousand seven hundred fifty-six.

lines.text: Most stubs show two columns: this pay period, and year-to-date.
lines.say: Most stubs show two columns: this pay period, and year to date.

lines.text: YTD adds up every check since January 1. By year's end, those totals should be close to your W-2.
lines.say: Y T D adds up every check since January first. By year's end, those totals should be close to your W-2.

lines.text: So YTD is where problems show up early, like a 401(k) deduction that never started.
lines.say: So Y T D is where problems show up early, like a four oh one k deduction that never started.

lines.text: The header matters too: your name, pay period, pay date, and often your W-4 filing status.
lines.say: The header matters too: your name, the pay period, the pay date, and often your W-4 filing status.

lines.text: The W-4 tells your employer how much federal income tax to hold back from each check.
lines.say: The W-4 tells your employer how much federal income tax to hold back from each check.

lines.text: Since 2020, the W-4 has no allowances. It's a five-step form covering other jobs, dependents and extra withholding.
lines.say: Since twenty twenty, the W-4 has no allowances. It's a five-step form covering other jobs, dependents and extra withholding.

lines.text: An older W-4 still counts if it was filed before 2020 and never changed. Either way, it drives the withholding line.
lines.say: An older W-4 still counts if it was filed before twenty twenty and never changed. Either way, it drives the withholding line.

lines.text: Chapter 2: The tax lines.
lines.say: Chapter two: the tax lines.

lines.text: Two of those taxes work like flat rates: Social Security and Medicare. Together, they're called FICA.
lines.say: Two of those taxes work like flat rates: Social Security and Medicare. Together, they're called FICA.

lines.text: In 2026, Social Security tax is 6.2% of your wages, and your employer quietly pays another 6.2%.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-six, Social Security tax is six point two percent of your wages, and your employer quietly pays another six point two percent.

lines.text: But it stops at a cap called the wage base. For 2026, the cap is $184,500.
lines.say: But it stops at a cap called the wage base. For twenty twenty-six, that cap is one hundred eighty-four thousand five hundred dollars.

lines.text: The cap follows average wages. It was $137,700 in 2020, and it's risen every year since.
lines.say: The cap follows average wages. It was one hundred thirty-seven thousand seven hundred dollars in twenty twenty, and it's risen every year since.

lines.text: The biggest jump in that stretch came in 2023: $13,200 in one year.
lines.say: The biggest jump in that stretch came in twenty twenty-three: thirteen thousand two hundred dollars in a single year.

lines.text: So in 2026, the most one employer withholds for Social Security is $11,439. Past the cap, that line drops to zero.
lines.say: So in twenty twenty-six, the most one employer withholds for Social Security is eleven thousand four hundred thirty-nine dollars. Past the cap, that line drops to zero.

lines.text: Medicare is different: 1.45% of every dollar you earn, with no cap.
lines.say: Medicare works differently. It's one point four five percent of every dollar you earn, with no cap at all.

lines.text: Past $200,000 of wages in a year, employers must withhold an extra 0.9%, whatever your filing status.
lines.say: And once wages pass two hundred thousand dollars in a year, employers must withhold an extra zero point nine percent, whatever your filing status.

lines.text: What you finally owe depends on filing status: $200,000 for single filers, $250,000 for married filing jointly. The tax return settles it.
lines.say: What you finally owe depends on filing status: two hundred thousand for single filers, two hundred fifty thousand for married filing jointly. The tax return settles it.

lines.text: Below the cap, those two add up to 7.65% of FICA wages on every check.
lines.say: Below the cap, those two add up to seven point six five percent of your FICA wages on every check.

lines.text: Federal income tax is the line that moves. It depends on your W-4, your pay and the brackets.
lines.say: Federal income tax is the line that moves. It depends on your W-4, your pay and the brackets.

lines.text: For 2026, a single filer gets a $16,100 standard deduction before any income tax applies.
lines.say: For twenty twenty-six, a single filer gets a sixteen thousand one hundred dollar standard deduction before any income tax applies.

lines.text: The first $12,400 of taxable income is taxed at 10%, and the next slice, up to $50,400, at 12%.
lines.say: The first twelve thousand four hundred dollars of taxable income is taxed at ten percent, and the next slice, up to fifty thousand four hundred, at twelve percent.

lines.text: Above that comes 22%, then higher rates. Each rate only hits the dollars inside its slice.
lines.say: Above that comes twenty-two percent, then higher rates. Each rate only hits the dollars inside its slice.

lines.text: Payroll uses IRS tables to spread that yearly tax across your paychecks.
lines.say: Payroll uses I R S tables to spread that yearly tax across your paychecks.

lines.text: Chapter 3: One paycheck, exact math.
lines.say: Chapter three: one paycheck, exact math.

lines.text: A hypothetical example: a single worker earning $60,000 a year, paid every two weeks, so 26 paychecks.
lines.say: This is a hypothetical example: a single worker earning sixty thousand dollars a year, paid every two weeks, so twenty-six paychecks.

lines.text: They put 5% in a traditional 401(k), pay $100 a check for health insurance, and live in Texas, with no state income tax.
lines.say: They put five percent in a traditional four oh one k, pay one hundred dollars a check for health insurance, and live in Texas, with no state income tax.

lines.text: Gross pay per check: $60,000 divided by 26 is $2,307.69.
lines.say: Gross pay per check is sixty thousand divided by twenty-six: two thousand three hundred seven dollars and sixty-nine cents.

lines.text: Pre-tax deductions come out first: $115.38 for the 5% 401(k), and $100 for health.
lines.say: Pre-tax deductions come out first: one hundred fifteen dollars and thirty-eight cents for the five percent four oh one k, and one hundred for health.

lines.text: Here's the key move. The health premium skips FICA. The 401(k) doesn't.
lines.say: Here's the key move. The health premium skips FICA. The four oh one k doesn't.

lines.text: So FICA wages are $2,307.69 minus the $100 premium: $2,207.69.
lines.say: So FICA wages are gross pay minus the one hundred dollar premium: two thousand two hundred seven dollars and sixty-nine cents.

lines.text: Social Security at 6.2% is $136.88. Medicare at 1.45% is $32.01. Together, $168.89 of FICA per check.
lines.say: Social Security at six point two percent is about one hundred thirty-seven dollars. Medicare at one point four five percent is about thirty-two. Together, about one hundred sixty-nine dollars of FICA per check.

lines.text: For income tax, both deductions come off, which leaves $2,092.31.
lines.say: For income tax, both deductions come off, which leaves two thousand ninety-two dollars and thirty-one cents.

lines.text: Over a year, that's $54,400. Minus the $16,100 standard deduction, it leaves $38,300 of taxable income.
lines.say: Over a year, that's fifty-four thousand four hundred. Minus the sixteen thousand one hundred standard deduction, it leaves thirty-eight thousand three hundred of taxable income.

lines.text: 10% of the first $12,400 is $1,240. 12% of the remaining $25,900 is $3,108.
lines.say: Ten percent of the first twelve thousand four hundred is one thousand two hundred forty dollars. Twelve percent of the remaining twenty-five thousand nine hundred is three thousand one hundred eight.

lines.text: That's an estimated $4,348 a year, about $167.23 a check. Actual withholding can differ a bit.
lines.say: That's an estimated four thousand three hundred forty-eight dollars a year, about one hundred sixty-seven a check. Actual withholding can differ a bit.

lines.text: Subtract everything, and $2,307.69 of gross becomes $1,756.19 of take-home pay.
lines.say: Subtract everything, and about two thousand three hundred eight dollars of gross becomes about one thousand seven hundred fifty-six of take-home pay.

lines.text: That's about 76% of gross. And $115.38 of the gap isn't gone. It's in the 401(k).
lines.say: That's about seventy-six percent of gross. And about one hundred fifteen dollars of the gap isn't gone. It's in the four oh one k.

lines.text: That's the trade-off. A traditional 401(k) cuts tax now and is taxed when withdrawn. A Roth is taxed now, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free.
lines.say: That's the trade-off. A traditional four oh one k cuts tax now and is taxed when withdrawn. A Roth is taxed now, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free.

lines.text: Neither is better for everyone. It comes down to your tax rate now versus later.
lines.say: Neither is better for everyone. It comes down to your tax rate now versus later.

lines.text: Chapter 4: The W-2, box by box.
lines.say: Chapter four: the W-2, box by box.

lines.text: Tax year 2026 W-2s are due to workers by February 1, 2027, because January 31 is a Sunday.
lines.say: Tax year twenty twenty-six W-2s are due to workers by February first, twenty twenty-seven, because January thirty-first is a Sunday.

lines.text: Box 1 is wages for federal income tax: $60,000, minus $3,000 of 401(k), minus $2,600 of premiums. That's $54,400.
lines.say: Box one is wages for federal income tax: sixty thousand, minus three thousand of four oh one k, minus two thousand six hundred of premiums. That's fifty-four thousand four hundred.

lines.text: Box 2 is the federal income tax withheld during the year.
lines.say: Box two is the federal income tax that was withheld during the year.

lines.text: Boxes 3 and 4 are Social Security wages and tax. Box 3 is $57,400, because the 401(k) still counts for FICA.
lines.say: Boxes three and four are Social Security wages and tax. Box three is fifty-seven thousand four hundred, because the four oh one k still counts for FICA.

lines.text: Boxes 5 and 6 are Medicare wages and tax. Box 5 usually matches Box 3, unless pay tops the Social Security cap.
lines.say: Boxes five and six are Medicare wages and tax. Box five usually matches box three, unless pay tops the Social Security cap.

lines.text: Mystery solved. Box 1 is $3,000 lower than Boxes 3 and 5: exactly the 401(k) money.
lines.say: Mystery solved. Box one is three thousand dollars lower than boxes three and five: exactly the four oh one k money.

lines.text: Quick math check: Box 4 should be 6.2% of Box 3. Here, that's $3,558.80.
lines.say: Quick math check: box four should be six point two percent of box three. Here, that's three thousand five hundred fifty-eight dollars and eighty cents.

lines.text: Box 6 should be 1.45% of Box 5: $832.30, give or take a few cents of rounding.
lines.say: Box six should be one point four five percent of box five: eight hundred thirty-two dollars and thirty cents, give or take rounding.

lines.text: Box 12 holds letter codes. Code D is traditional 401(k) deferrals: $3,000 here. Employer matches don't appear.
lines.say: Box twelve holds letter codes. Code D is traditional four oh one k deferrals: three thousand dollars here. Employer matches don't appear.

lines.text: Code AA is Roth 401(k) money. It's after-tax, so it stays inside Box 1.
lines.say: Code double A is Roth four oh one k money. It's after-tax, so it stays inside box one.

lines.text: Code W is HSA money that went in through payroll. It's already left out of Boxes 1, 3 and 5.
lines.say: Code W is H S A money that went in through payroll. It's already left out of boxes one, three and five.

lines.text: Code DD is the total cost of your employer health plan, both shares. It's information only, not taxable.
lines.say: Code double D is the total cost of your employer health plan, both shares. It's information only, not taxable.

lines.text: DD can be a big number, so it scares people. It's a receipt, not income.
lines.say: Double D can be a big number, so it scares people. It's a receipt, not income.

lines.text: W-2s for tax year 2026 add new codes: TT for qualified overtime, only the extra half of time-and-a-half, and TP for cash tips reported to the employer.
lines.say: W-2s for tax year twenty twenty-six add new codes: T T for qualified overtime, only the extra half of time and a half, and T P for cash tips reported to the employer.

lines.text: And TA shows employer contributions to a Trump account. The tip and overtime deductions are set to run from 2025 through 2028.
lines.say: And T A shows employer contributions to a Trump account. The tip and overtime deductions are set to run from twenty twenty-five through twenty twenty-eight.

lines.text: Further down, Boxes 15 through 20 tell the same story for state and local tax.
lines.say: Further down, boxes fifteen through twenty tell the same story for state and local tax.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Common mistakes.
lines.say: Chapter five: common mistakes.

lines.text: Mistake one: expecting Box 1 to equal your salary. With pre-tax deductions, it usually won't, and that's normal.
lines.say: Mistake one: expecting box one to equal your salary. With pre-tax deductions, it usually won't, and that's normal.

lines.text: Mistake two: ignoring YTD, where a missing 401(k) deduction or a wrong premium shows up early.
lines.say: Mistake two: ignoring Y T D, where a missing four oh one k deduction or a wrong premium shows up early.

lines.text: Mistake three: skipping the basics. A wrong name or Social Security number can slow down a tax return.
lines.say: Mistake three: skipping the basics. A wrong name or Social Security number can slow down a tax return.

lines.text: Mistake four: treating code DD as income. It isn't taxable.
lines.say: Mistake four: treating code double D as income. It isn't taxable.

lines.text: Bonus mistake: an old W-4 after marriage or a second job. The form doesn't update itself, so withholding can drift.
lines.say: Bonus mistake: an old W-4 after marriage or a second job. The form doesn't update itself, so withholding can drift.

lines.text: Past the $184,500 wage base, the Social Security line drops to zero for the year. That's the cap, not a glitch.
lines.say: Past the one hundred eighty-four thousand five hundred dollar wage base, the Social Security line drops to zero for the year. That's the cap, not a glitch.

lines.text: If a W-2 is wrong, the first step is asking the employer for a corrected form, called a W-2c.
lines.say: So what if a W-2 is wrong? The first step is asking the employer for a corrected form, called a W-2c.

lines.text: If it's still missing or wrong at the end of February, the IRS can be contacted. It sends the employer a letter.
lines.say: If it's still missing or wrong at the end of February, the I R S can be contacted, and it sends the employer a letter.

lines.text: If the filing deadline comes first, Form 4852 serves as a substitute W-2, and an amended return can fix things later.
lines.say: If the filing deadline comes first, Form forty-eight fifty-two serves as a substitute W-2, and an amended return can fix things later.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Recap and checklist.
lines.say: Chapter six: recap and checklist.

lines.text: In 2026, Social Security is 6.2% up to $184,500. Medicare is 1.45%, plus 0.9% over $200,000.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-six, Social Security is six point two percent up to one hundred eighty-four thousand five hundred dollars. Medicare is one point four five percent, plus zero point nine over two hundred thousand.

lines.text: On the W-2, Box 1 is for income tax, Boxes 3 and 5 for FICA, and a traditional 401(k) explains the gap.
lines.say: On the W-2, box one is for income tax, boxes three and five for FICA, and a traditional four oh one k explains the gap.

lines.text: A pay stub shows one check. The W-2 shows the whole year, sorted by tax.
lines.say: A pay stub shows one check. The W-2 shows the whole year, sorted by tax.

lines.text: And here's the one-screen checklist. One: gross pay matches the salary or hours for that period.
lines.say: And here's the one-screen checklist. One: gross pay matches the salary or the hours for that period.

lines.text: Two: each pre-tax deduction matches what was elected, like the 401(k) percent and the premium.
lines.say: Two: each pre-tax deduction matches what was elected, like the four oh one k percent and the premium.

lines.text: Three: Social Security is 6.2% of FICA wages up to the cap, and Medicare is 1.45% with no cap.
lines.say: Three: Social Security is six point two percent of FICA wages up to the cap, and Medicare is one point four five percent with no cap.

lines.text: Four: the W-2 has the right name and Social Security number, and its boxes line up with the last stub's YTD.
lines.say: Four: the W-2 has the right name and Social Security number, and its boxes line up with the last stub's year-to-date totals.

lines.text: So when a W-2 shows three different wages, now you know why. All three are right.
lines.say: So when a W-2 shows three different wages, now you know why. All three are right.

lines.text: That's the money. Follow for more.
lines.say: That's the money. Follow for more.

post.yt_desc:
Your W-2 can show three different wages, and all three are right. This guide walks through a pay stub from gross pay to net pay, the 2026 payroll tax rules (Social Security 6.2% up to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45% plus 0.9% withheld over $200,000), and a hypothetical $60,000 biweekly paycheck with exact math ($2,307.69 gross to $1,756.19 net). Then it reads the W-2 box by box, including why Box 1 is lower than Boxes 3 and 5, Box 12 codes D, AA, W and DD, the new 2026 codes TT, TP and TA, the common mistakes, and a one-screen checklist.

CHAPTERS

Sources: Social Security Administration, contribution and benefit base 2020-2026 (announced October 2025); IRS Topic 560, Additional Medicare Tax; IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026 standard deduction and brackets); IRS 401(k) contribution limits for 2026; IRS FAQs on the 2020 Form W-4; IRS 2026 General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3; Bureau of Labor Statistics, length of pay period (February 2023); Nolo, missing or incorrect W-2.

News and education, not financial advice.
